lesson.subject: english
lesson.title: Neat Joined-Up Handwriting
lesson.summary: Practise joining letters with lead-ins so writing is neat and flowing.
learning_objectives: Make the first, second and third joins
Keep letter size and spacing even

standards.text: Form lower-case letters of the correct size relative to one another; start using diagonal and horizontal strokes needed to join letters

success_criteria: I can sit letters on the baseline
I can make the first, second and third joins
I can write a neat note
lesson.real_life: English joined script and Urdu calligraphy as two ways of flowing writing, and a thank-you note to a teacher.

warm_up.prompt: A neat note is easier to read.
warm_up.explanation: Neat writing is easier to read.

blocks.markdown: Today's big question: how do we join letters neatly?
blocks.say: Today we make our writing flow. How do we join letters so they hold hands?

blocks.alt: Joined-up handwriting in black ink on lined paper with stripes of shadow across it
blocks.caption: Joined-up writing flows because the pencil stays on the page.
blocks.credit: Photo by Micah Boswell on Unsplash
blocks.say: This writing flows along the page. Many of the letters are joined together.

blocks.markdown: The **baseline** is the line that letters sit on.
blocks.say: Letters sit on an invisible line. We call it the baseline.

blocks.markdown: The **x-height** is the height of small letters.
blocks.say: Small letters like a, e, o and n reach the x-height. That is the middle zone.

scenes.caption: Baseline.
scenes.say: The baseline is the bottom line. Letters sit on it like toys on a shelf.

scenes.caption: x-height.
scenes.say: Small letters like a and n fill the middle. That is the x-height.

scenes.caption: Ascenders.
scenes.say: Tall letters like b and d reach higher. They have ascenders.

question.hint: Think of toys on a shelf.

options.text: The line that letters sit on

blocks.text: Stop 2: Lead-in and the first join

blocks.markdown: A **lead-in** starts a letter. A **lead-out** leaves it.
blocks.say: A lead-in is a small stroke before a letter. It starts the join.
After a letter, the lead-out swings up to meet the next letter. That is a join.

scenes.caption: Lead-in.
scenes.say: Start on the baseline with a little lead-in. Then write the letter.

scenes.caption: Lead-out.
scenes.say: Finish the letter with a lead-out. The pencil stays on the page.

scenes.caption: First join.
scenes.say: The first join goes diagonally up, as in in. The letters hold hands.

question.prompt: A lead-in is a small stroke that starts a letter.

blocks.title: Sam's thank-you note
blocks.transcript: Sam wants to say thank you to his teacher. He sits his letters on the baseline. Each letter starts with a tiny lead-in. His letters hold hands. The pencil does not lift. He leaves a finger space between words. He checks for gaps and floating letters. His note is neat and easy to read. His teacher smiles. She loves the note!
blocks.caption: Sam writes a joined-up thank-you note to his teacher.

blocks.say: Let us remember. Letters sit on the baseline. Lead-ins and lead-outs make joins.

blocks.markdown: The **first join** goes diagonally up to a small letter.
blocks.say: The first join goes diagonally up to a small letter. Try in, ig, ed, eg, an and ar.

blocks.markdown: The **second join** goes up to a tall letter.
blocks.say: The second join goes up to a tall letter. Try ck and ch.

scenes.caption: First join: in.
scenes.say: In the word in, the first join goes from i up to n.

scenes.caption: Second join: ch.
scenes.say: In ch, the second join goes up to a tall letter, h.

scenes.caption: Do not lift.
scenes.say: Keep the pencil moving. Do not lift it inside a word.

question.prompt: Which pair uses the first join?
question.hint: It goes diagonally up to a small letter.

blocks.alt: A fountain pen nib resting on lined paper beside joined handwriting
blocks.caption: A pen nib glides across the lines in joined-up writing.
blocks.credit: Photo by Aaron Burden on Unsplash
blocks.say: This pen writes on lined paper. Its nib glides along without lifting.

blocks.markdown: The **third join** goes across from o.
blocks.say: The third join starts from the letter o. It goes straight across. Try on, om and ow.

blocks.title: Which join?
blocks.goal: Move each pair. Diagonal to a small letter goes in First. Across from o goes in Third.
blocks.say: Now sort the pairs. Which join does each use?

blocks.title: Practise joins
instructions: Write in, ig and ed with the first join.
Write ck and ch with the second join.
Write on, om and ow with the third join.

question.prompt: Which pair uses the third join?
question.explanation: On starts from o and goes across.

points: First join: diagonal up to a small letter
Second join: up to a tall letter
blocks.say: Let us remember. First join goes up to a small letter. Second goes up to a tall letter. Third goes across from o.

mini_quiz.explanation: The third join starts from o.

blocks.markdown: A **broken join** leaves a gap between letters.
blocks.say: A broken join leaves a gap. Look for letters that float.

scenes.caption: A gap.
scenes.say: This word has a gap between letters. The pencil was lifted.

scenes.caption: Floating.
scenes.say: This letter floats above the baseline. It is not sitting on the line.

scenes.caption: Neat.
scenes.say: Neat writing has even letters and equal gaps between words.

blocks.markdown: Copy a **model** line, then write your own.
blocks.say: Now use your joins in a real note. First copy a short line carefully.

blocks.markdown: Many writing styles flow along a line.
blocks.say: English joined script and Urdu calligraphy are two ways of flowing writing.
Both need patience, even shapes and a steady hand.

blocks.markdown: A note can say thank you.

scenes.caption: Write.
